items.title: The Governor — office, powers and assent to bills
items.body:
The **Governor** is the constitutional (nominal) head of the state under **Article 153**, appointed by the President (**Art 155**) for a five-year term held **during the President's pleasure** (**Art 156**). A Governor must be a citizen of India, at least **35 years** old, and not a member of any legislature or holder of an office of profit.

**Categories of power**
- **Executive (Art 154):** all state executive action runs in the Governor's name; appoints the CM and ministers, the Advocate General (Art 165), the State Election Commissioner and members of the SPSC; is Chancellor of state universities.
- **Legislative:** summons, prorogues and dissolves the legislature; addresses it; nominates expert members to the Council and (until the 104th Amendment) one Anglo-Indian to the Assembly.
- **Financial:** money bills need his prior recommendation; oversees the state budget and the state Finance Commission.
- **Judicial (Art 161):** can pardon, reprieve, remit or commute sentences under **state law**, but **cannot pardon a death sentence** and has **no** court-martial powers.

**Assent to bills (Art 200 & 201)**

| Option under Art 200 | Effect |
|---|---|
| Assent | Bill becomes law |
| Withhold assent | Bill ends |
| Return (not money bill) | Legislature reconsiders; if re-passed, Governor must assent |
| Reserve for President | Art 201 applies |

The Supreme Court (2023, Punjab Governor case) held that a Governor withholding assent must **return the bill with reasons** and cannot sit on it indefinitely.
keyPoints: Governor = constitutional head of the state (Art 153); appointed by the President (Art 155) for 5 years, during President's pleasure (Art 156).
Minimum age 35; must not be a legislator or hold an office of profit.
Executive actions run in the Governor's name (Art 154); he appoints CM, ministers, Advocate General, SEC and SPSC members; is Chancellor of universities.
Art 200: Governor may assent, withhold, return (non-money bills) or reserve a bill for the President; if a returned bill is re-passed he must assent.
Pardoning power (Art 161) covers state law only; the Governor cannot pardon a death sentence and has no court-martial power.
104th Amendment (2019) ended nomination of an Anglo-Indian member to state Assemblies.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — State Government: Governor (Articles 153-161, 200-201)

items.title: Governor's ordinance power and discretion vs the President
items.body:
The Governor's **ordinance-making power (Article 213)** mirrors the President's (Art 123) but with an extra check.

**Ordinances (Art 213)**
- Promulgated only when the assembly (unicameral) or **neither House** (bicameral) is in session.
- Coextensive with the state legislature's law-making power; ceases **six weeks** after reassembly (or earlier if disapproved).
- Uniquely, the Governor needs the **President's instructions** in certain cases (e.g. bills that would need reservation).

**Discretionary powers**
Unlike the President, the Governor has real **discretion** in defined situations: appointing a CM when no party has a clear majority, dismissing a CM who has lost confidence, reserving a bill for the President, and recommending **President's Rule (Art 356)**. Under **Art 163**, if a question arises whether a matter is within his discretion, the Governor's decision is final.

The **Sarkaria (1988)** and **Punchhi (2010)** Commissions recommended appointing non-partisan Governors, using Art 356 sparingly, and following a clear floor-test procedure — themes central to recurring Centre-State tensions.
keyPoints: Art 213: Governor promulgates ordinances only when the House(s) are not in session; they lapse 6 weeks after reassembly.
Governor's ordinance power needs the President's instructions in certain cases — a check the President does not face.
Governor's discretion: choosing a CM in a hung assembly, dismissing a CM without majority, reserving bills, recommending President's Rule (Art 356).
Art 163: the Governor's decision on what falls within his discretion is final and non-justiciable.
Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions urged non-partisan Governors and sparing use of Article 356.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ordinance & discretionary powers of Governor; Sarkaria/Punchhi Commissions

items.title: Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers
items.body:
The **Chief Minister** is the real executive authority and head of the state government, appointed by the Governor under **Article 164**. The Constitution lays down no procedure; by convention the Governor invites the leader of the majority party, or in a hung assembly uses discretion and asks for a floor test.

**Council of Ministers**
- **Art 163:** a Council of Ministers headed by the CM aids and advises the Governor.
- **Art 164:** the CM is appointed by the Governor; other ministers are appointed on the CM's advice; ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure.
- **91st Amendment (2003):** total ministers (incl. CM) **≤ 15%** of the Assembly's strength, **minimum 12**; a member disqualified for defection cannot be a minister.
- **Art 177:** ministers may speak in either House but vote only in the House they belong to.
- Three ranks: **Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers**.

**Responsibility**
- **Collective:** the Council is collectively responsible to the **Legislative Assembly**; a no-confidence motion forces **all** ministers to resign, including those from the Council.
- **Individual:** ministers hold office at the Governor's pleasure, but he removes a minister only on the CM's advice. There is **no legal responsibility** of ministers (unlike Britain).
keyPoints: CM appointed by the Governor under Art 164; real executive authority and head of government.
Art 163 = Council aids and advises the Governor; advice is not enquirable in court.
91st Amendment 2003: ministers (incl. CM) ≤ 15% of Assembly strength, minimum 12; defectors barred from ministership.
Three ranks — Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers; only Cabinet Ministers form the Cabinet.
Collective responsibility is to the Legislative Assembly; a no-confidence motion makes all ministers resign.
A non-member can be made a minister but must become a legislator within six months.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Chief Minister & State Council of Ministers (Articles 163, 164, 177)

items.title: State Legislature — structure, Assembly and Council
items.body:
The **State Legislature** is governed by **Part VI, Articles 168-212**. It may be **unicameral** (Assembly only) or **bicameral** (Assembly + Council). **Article 168** lists the bicameral states; **Article 169** lets Parliament create or abolish a Council on a **special-majority resolution** of the Assembly (treated as ordinary law, not an Art 368 amendment).

**Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha)**
- Directly elected; **Art 170**: max **500**, min **60** members (Goa, Sikkim fewer).
- Tenure **5 years** (**Art 172**), dissolvable earlier by the Governor; extendable by one year during a national emergency.

**Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)**
- **Art 171:** strength **≤ one-third** of the Assembly (min **40**); a **permanent body** — one-third retire every two years; members serve six years.

| Council category | Share |
|---|---|
| Elected by MLAs | 1/3 |
| Elected by local bodies | 1/3 |
| Elected by graduates | 1/12 |
| Elected by teachers | 1/12 |
| Nominated by Governor | 1/6 |

Thus **5/6 are elected** and **1/6 nominated**. A Money Bill can be introduced **only in the Assembly**; the Council may only recommend amendments (returned within 14 days). Collective control over the executive (questions, motions, no-confidence) rests with the **Assembly**.
keyPoints: State legislature = Part VI, Articles 168-212; can be unicameral or bicameral.
Art 169: Parliament creates/abolishes a Council on the Assembly's special-majority resolution; not an Art 368 amendment.
Assembly (Art 170): max 500, min 60 members; tenure 5 years (Art 172).
Council (Art 171): a permanent body, one-third retire every two years, six-year terms; strength ≤ 1/3 of Assembly (min 40).
Council composition: 1/3 MLAs, 1/3 local bodies, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated — 5/6 elected, 1/6 nominated.
Money Bills originate only in the Assembly; the Council can only recommend amendments; no joint sitting at state level.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — State Legislature (Articles 168-212)

items.title: Membership — qualifications, disqualifications and defection
items.body:
**Qualifications (Constitution + RPA 1951)**
- Citizen of India; **25 years** for the Assembly, **30 years** for the Council.
- Must be an elector for an assembly constituency in the state; other qualifications as prescribed by Parliament.

**Disqualifications**
- Holding an office of profit (except minister/exempted offices), being of unsound mind, an undischarged insolvent, not a citizen, or disqualified under any parliamentary law.
- Under the RPA 1951: conviction for certain election or serious offences (2+ years' imprisonment), failure to file election expenses, or government-contract interest.

**Anti-defection (Tenth Schedule)**
- A member disqualified for **defection** is decided by the **Speaker** (Assembly) or **Chairman** (Council) — **not** the Governor; the 1992 Supreme Court ruling made this **subject to judicial review**.

**Section 8(4) RPA** — struck down by the Supreme Court in 2013 (*Lily Thomas*), so a convicted legislator is disqualified **from the date of conviction**, ending the earlier protection during appeal.

A seat is also vacated by double membership, resignation, 60-day unauthorised absence, court-voided election, expulsion, or on election as President/Vice-President or appointment as Governor.
keyPoints: Age: 25 years for the Assembly, 30 years for the Council; must be a citizen and an elector in the state.
Disqualified for office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency, non-citizenship, or under parliamentary law.
Defection disqualification (Tenth Schedule) decided by the Speaker/Chairman, not the Governor.
1992 SC ruling: the presiding officer's defection decision is subject to judicial review.
Section 8(4) RPA struck down in 2013 — disqualification runs from the date of conviction.
Seat vacated by double membership, resignation, 60-day absence, void election, expulsion, or becoming Governor/President/VP.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — State Legislature: qualifications, disqualifications, Tenth Schedule & RPA 1951

items.title: Andhra Pradesh angle — Assembly, Council and Governor
items.body:
Andhra Pradesh has a **bicameral** legislature seated at **Amaravati**.

**Legislative Assembly**
- Elected strength **175 members** (down from 294 in the undivided state before the 2014 bifurcation, when Telangana got 119).
- Directly elected; tenure five years (Art 172); three sessions a year (Budget, Monsoon, Winter).

**Legislative Council (Sasana Mandali)**
- **58 seats** — roughly one-third of the Assembly, satisfying Art 171.
- A telling case study of **Article 169**: the Council existed **1958-1985**, was **abolished in 1985** (under N. T. Rama Rao's government), and was **revived in 2007** (under Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy) — showing how a Council can be created or abolished through an Assembly resolution and a parliamentary Act.

**Governor & executive**
- The Governor of AP is the constitutional head (Art 153); the Chief Minister (leader of the majority party in the 175-member Assembly) heads the real executive.
- AP illustrates the Governor's Art 200 assent role, Art 213 ordinances and Art 356 recommendation power in a state-level setting.
keyPoints: AP has a bicameral legislature at Amaravati: Assembly 175 seats, Legislative Council 58 seats.
Undivided AP Assembly had 294 seats; after the 2014 bifurcation AP has 175 and Telangana 119.
AP Legislative Council existed 1958-1985, was abolished in 1985, and was revived in 2007 — a textbook Article 169 case.
The 58-seat Council is about one-third of the 175-member Assembly, consistent with Article 171.
AP's CM is the leader of the majority party in the 175-member Assembly; the Governor is the constitutional head (Art 153).
items.source: Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly & Legislative Council — verified online (Sep 2026); Article 169

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Legislature & Executive — State Snapshot (2026)
items.body:
## Executive

- **Governor:** Justice (Retd) **S. Abdul Nazeer** (former SC judge), in office since **24 Feb 2023**; Raj Bhavan at **Vijayawada**. Nominal head; real power with the CM and Council of Ministers (Art 163–164).
- **Chief Minister & Council of Ministers:** appointed by the Governor (Art 164); collectively responsible to the Assembly.

## Legislature (bicameral, Amaravati region)

| House | Strength | Presiding officer | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legislative Assembly | **175** elected | Speaker | Dissolvable; 5-yr term (Art 172) |
| Legislative Council | **58** (50 elected + 8 nominated) | Chairman | Permanent (Art 171); 1/3 retire every 2 yrs |

- **Council history:** existed 1958–1985, **abolished in 1985**, **revived in 2007**. A fresh **abolition resolution (2020)** by the Assembly was sent to the Centre but no Act of Parliament followed, and it was **later not pursued/withdrawn** — the Council continues.

## President's Rule (Art 356) in AP

- **1973** — Jai Andhra agitation.
- **2014** — political impasse before bifurcation.
keyPoints: AP Governor (Sep 2026): Justice (Retd) S. Abdul Nazeer, since 24 Feb 2023, Raj Bhavan Vijayawada
AP Assembly = 175 elected seats; Speaker presides; 5-year term (Art 172)
AP Legislative Council = 58 seats (50 elected + 8 nominated); permanent house; Chairman presides
AP Council abolished 1985, revived 2007; 2020 abolition resolution never enacted and later dropped
President's Rule in AP imposed in 1973 (Jai Andhra) and 2014 (pre-bifurcation)
items.source: Official AP Govt / Constitution; incumbents verified via Wikipedia (Governor of AP, AP Legislative Council) as of Sep 2026

items.title: Chief Secretary, Governor's Immunity & Speaker on Dissolution
items.body:
**Chief Secretary:** the administrative head of the State secretariat is **appointed by the Chief Minister** (not the Governor) and has **no fixed statutory tenure**.

**Governor's immunity (Art 361):** during the term of office the Governor is **not answerable to any court** for the exercise of powers, and **no criminal proceedings** can be instituted or continued against the Governor.

**Speaker on dissolution:** the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly **does not vacate office on dissolution**; he continues **until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly**.
keyPoints: The Chief Secretary is appointed by the Chief Minister and has no fixed statutory tenure.
Under Art 361 the Governor enjoys immunity from criminal proceedings during the term of office.
The Assembly Speaker continues in office after dissolution until just before the first meeting of the new Assembly.
